tasks.name: Smaller packages: only the locale data a reader needs
tasks.description:
Asked by the user (2026-10-30): don't carry locale data a reader never uses; keep the packages as small as they can be.

**Today.** The processor formats by CLDR (`md.date`, `md.number`, `md.currency`, …, for `md.lang`) with ICU4X's compiled data for every locale (`icu` 2.4.0 in `processor/Cargo.toml`), so every language formats offline. All of it is inside `@compmd/processor`'s WebAssembly: 808 KB gzipped, a tarball of 844 KB.

**First, measure** how much of the WebAssembly is locale data (a build with only `en`, against today's), so the choice rests on numbers.

**The alternatives to weigh, then settle with the user:**

1. **Two builds**: a small one with a few locales (`en`, `tr` and the most used few more, the list to settle), and a full one with all of CLDR, for example `@compmd/processor` and `@compmd/processor-full`, or a Cargo feature for the crate.
2. **Locale data as separate packages**: one processor without locale data (or with `en` only), and the data for other locales loaded when a document's `md.lang` needs it (ICU4X's blob data, per locale or per group, for example `@compmd/locale-tr`), cached like any module.
3. A mix: the small build with its locales compiled in, and the others loadable.

For each: the sizes (gzipped, the WebAssembly and the tarball), what a host does to use it, what a document in a locale that isn't there shows (a fallback locale and a diagnostic, which may need a change to the spec's formatting functions), offline use, the crate's features, and what the release workflow publishes.

**Then** implement the chosen one: the build, the packages, the website and playground on the right build, READMEs and `RELEASING.md`, tests for a missing locale, sizes in the bench.

## From earlier work

- The WebAssembly is about 946 KB gzipped now.
- The measurement needs an English-only build of ICU4X's data, made with ICU4X's `icu4x-datagen` tool (`cargo install icu4x-datagen`), used only to generate the data for the measurement, nothing added to the project. The user put the task in the backlog (2026-11-17) before it was installed: ask for the go to install it when the task is taken again, then bring the numbers and the three options for the user to choose from.

tasks.name: Any npm package as published, through a module loader (K2)
tasks.description:
Later work from the accepted design of packs from a registry (`docs/packs-from-a-registry.md`, R7 K2, R9 *Why not any npm package as it is published?*). The user would rather shared libraries were plain npm packages than library packs. That needs a module loader in the frames resolving Node's rules (`exports`, `module`, bare imports between packages) over a package's whole dependency tree, with no WebAssembly under the strict policy; CommonJS packages refused. Pack chunks (R7) come with the same loader.

**First a design doc**, reviewed with the user, with a spike if the loader's cost is unclear (d3 7.9: more than 31 packages on a first visit). Then the spec and implementation tasks.

## From earlier work

A draft design is committed, not yet approved: `docs/npm-packages.md` (compmd `3f30a02`). It proposes ES module packages named in `peerDependencies`, the registry resolving the tree with the policy, bundled once in the compile frame (Rollup browser build) instead of a loader in every frame (K2), cached by integrities; CommonJS refused (W121). A spike first (d3, a chart's part, Mermaid); after approval, the spike, then the spec and build tasks. The user put the task in the backlog (2026-11-17); start from the draft when it is taken again.

tasks.name: A pandoc reader, so pandoc turns CompMD documents into PDF, Word, EPUB
tasks.description:
A way for pandoc to read CompMD documents, so authors and hosts turn them into anything pandoc writes: PDF (through LaTeX or Typst), Word, EPUB, HTML. Proposed by the user on 2026-11-02, while the site's PDFs were being made, as something wanted for the future anyway.

## Background
- The guides and the spec are plain GitHub Markdown, not CompMD: pandoc's own `gfm` reader already reads them, so the site's PDFs don't need this. They are printed with Chrome, which keeps the site's look; pandoc would give book typography and page numbers in the contents instead.
- A CompMD document needs the processor: imports, definitions, `if`/`each`, interpolation and layout only mean something after it expands them (spec §12.3).

## Design first (a design document, reviewed with the user, before code)
Never reimplement the syntax (no Lua parser of CompMD): build on the processor, so pandoc gets what the spec says.
- **The bridge:** the processor's expanded tree, translated to pandoc's JSON AST. Where it lives: a small CLI (`compmd pandoc doc.comp.md | pandoc -f json -o doc.pdf`, from the Rust crate), and/or a pandoc custom reader in Lua that calls it (`pandoc -f compmd.lua doc.comp.md -o doc.pdf`), and/or the wasm package for JS hosts.
- **The mapping:** mdast nodes to pandoc's (most map one to one: headings, lists, tables, code, math, footnotes, alerts as Divs); `box` and the layout built-ins as pandoc Divs with their params as attributes, so a pandoc filter or a template styles them; host-language components as their fallback (spec §4.5), since pandoc runs no code; inputs as their current value, as a processor that isn't interactive shows them (spec §8.7); a rendered code block (spec §7.7) as its code block, or its `alt`.
- **What the request carries:** the document's files, data and packs, as for any processor (`process` and its request); the inputs from the command line.
- **Diagnostics:** printed as the processor's, with a strict mode that fails on an F (spec §10.1).
- **Testing:** the conformance set's expanded trees through the bridge, and a few documents to PDF and DOCX in CI (pandoc and Typst are small to install; LaTeX is large).

## Not in this task
Using it for the site's own PDFs; layout fidelity beyond what pandoc's Divs and a template can give.

## From earlier work

A draft design is committed, not yet approved: `docs/pandoc.md` (compmd `8f1d683`, revised in `83a25eb` after the user's review: components as they print, use cases, its own repository `comp-markdown/compmd-pandoc`). It proposes the expanded tree written as pandoc JSON by a new `compmd-pandoc` crate; a `compmd pandoc` command (a new `compmd-cli`) and a Lua reader; the mapping (boxes as Divs, host components as fallbacks, inputs as values, frontmatter as metadata); packs, data and inputs from flags; tests over the conformance set and PDF/DOCX via Typst. The user put the task in the backlog (2026-11-17); start from the draft when it is taken again, and build after approval.

tasks.name: Find unused dependencies and exports, with a tool
tasks.description:
Found in an earlier scan of the repository (2026-11-06): two of its checks couldn't be done well by reading files one by one.

## What is left
- **Unused dependencies** in the `package.json` files of create-pack, devtools, editor, editor/packs/minimermaid, guides, pack, packs/mermaid, registry, render, sandbox, vite, wasm, website and website/app, and in the `Cargo.toml` files of `processor` and `wasm`. (The root `package.json` has none.)
- **Unused TypeScript exports**: exported functions, classes and types that nothing imports and that aren't part of a package's public entry. (Rust needs no such check: clippy's `dead_code` already fails on unused crate-private items.)

## Why it needs a decision
Both need a tool that sees the whole repository: [knip](https://knip.dev) for the TypeScript packages, [cargo-machete](https://github.com/bnjbvr/cargo-machete) or `cargo udeps` for the crates. Running one, even once through `pnpm dlx`, runs code from outside the repository, which the session's permissions refused. To decide:
1. Add knip (and cargo-machete) as dev tools, perhaps run in `cargo make ci` so the debt doesn't come back; or
2. Run them once by hand, outside an agent session, and file what they find; or
3. Drop the check.

## Then
Remove what is unused, with no change in behaviour; `cargo make ci` and `pnpm -r lint` green.

tasks.name: Make a table's rows from data (analyse the options first)
tasks.description:
Found while writing the website's table example (2026-11-06): a document can't make a table's rows from data. The author wanted each city's row of a GFM table made by an `each` over a data file; today the rows have to be written out.

## Why it can't today
- `each` joins what its body makes with `join=list` (a one-item list body, the copies one list) or `join=inline` (one line, with `sep=` and `last=`). Neither makes a table.
- A table row is a line of a GFM table, and a component line can't stand among a table's lines, so an `each` can't sit between the rows either.

## To analyse, before deciding
Options and their trade-offs, each tried on real documents (a table of cities, a changelog table, a price list), in CompMD and in a plain renderer:
- `join=table` on `each`: the body a one-row table, header included; the copies become one table, the header once. How headers that differ are reported, what `:: #empty` gives, alignment rows.
- A built-in table component (`::: table {rows=(…)}` with columns declared), and how it degrades.
- A template slot of a container that makes rows.
- Leaving tables to host-language components, and saying so.

## Then
The chosen option settled with the user, written into the spec with conformance cases, implemented in the processor, and the website's table example (`website/content/weather.comp.md`) made from data with it.

tasks.name: Wrapping an npm package as a pack, the design
tasks.description:
Asked by the user (2026-11-08): wrapping an existing npm package (a React, Svelte or plain JS/TS component) as a CompMD pack should be extremely easy.

## The design note
In `docs/`, decisions first, reviewed with the user before anything is built:
- **The least repetition in a pack,** so that updating to the package's next version is a version bump and little else: what a pack must state (signatures, fallbacks, demos) and what can be derived from the package itself (its TypeScript prop types, its `package.json`, its exports).
- **One command to generate a pack** from a package name, if it can be done (for example `npm create @compmd/pack --from <package>`): what it writes, what it asks, what it can't infer.
- How it fits `create-pack`'s templates (`leaf`, `renderer`, `library`), [writing a pack](docs/writing-a-pack.md), [packs from a registry](docs/packs-from-a-registry.md) and CMD-2 (any npm package through a module loader).
- Try it on three real packages of different kinds before the review, and list the gaps.

Each push needs the user's go.

## From earlier work

Not started: it is left for a session with the user, since its design is reviewed together.

tasks.name: State a component keeps, the design (and the spec)
tasks.description:
Asked by the user, 2026-11-10. An interactive drawing in a document (an Excalidraw diagram the reader draws in place) has **state the component itself manages**: the drawing, which isn't a param the author writes and isn't an input (spec §8.7: values of a few types the document reads). Today a component only gets params and slots and can `set` its bound inputs (spec §7.4), so a drawing has nowhere to live.

## Questions to settle, with examples
- **Where the state lives:** in the document (a fenced block the component owns, the way a signature fence belongs to a component), beside it (a file, like an image the document links), or in the host's storage, named from the document.
- **The likeness to attachments:** a drawing is a file the document owns, as an image is; can one mechanism serve both (a component's own files, which a host stores the way it stores a document's images and attachments)?
- **The host contract:** what the component gets (its state, a way to save it, size limits), when it saves (debounced, on close), and conflicts when two people draw at once.
- **Trust and safety:** a strict component may write only its own state, never other content; what a plain Markdown renderer shows (spec §14: a fallback image or text).
- **Full screen:** whether a component may ask the host to show it full screen, and how the host keeps it a document's content (spec §15).

## Do
A topic design in `docs/`, with real example documents and the spec change it needs (§7.4, §8.7, §14, §15, with a CHANGELOG entry), reviewed with the user. How an application that hosts CompMD stores such state is that application's own decision, once CompMD's design is accepted.

An npm package in `packs/`, built like [the Mermaid pack](docs/mermaid-pack.md) (`@compmd/pack`, one built module under the size cap, its licences published, light and dark following the page).

- What a plain renderer and a host without the state feature show: the fallback the design chose (an exported image or text).

## Tests

tasks.name: The registry rules in compmd-host, used by @compmd/registry as WebAssembly
tasks.description:
[Hosting](docs/hosting.md) H1, option (c): one implementation of the registry rules, in Rust. The resolver's loop, ranges as the processor matches them, the policy before any download, the integrity checks and the tar reader move into `compmd-host` (an HTTP client and a cache from its host, as traits), with a WebAssembly build that `@compmd/registry` uses; `@compmd/registry` keeps `fetch`, Cache Storage, the proxy and its API. Then the Tauri plugin's `registry/` proxy for apps that process in the page ([its decision 11](docs/tauri-plugin.md)).

## Tests
`@compmd/registry`'s tests run unchanged against the WebAssembly build; the crate's own tests share their fixtures.

## From earlier work

The user put the task in the backlog (2026-11-17); two points are settled with the user when it is taken again:

- **New Rust dependencies:** `miniz_oxide` (gunzip, pure Rust), `sha2` and `base64` (integrity), and for the WebAssembly build `wasm-bindgen`, `wasm-bindgen-futures` and `js-sys` (the async resolver over the host's `fetch`). The tar reader written by hand, as `registry/src/tar.ts` is.
- **The split:** it is three pieces of work: (1) the rules in `compmd-host` with HTTP and cache traits and shared fixtures, (2) the WebAssembly build and `@compmd/registry` on it, (3) the Tauri plugin's `registry/` proxy. Split into three tasks in that order (recommended), or keep one.

tasks.name: A tree-sitter grammar
tasks.description:
Asked by the user (2026-11-16): a tree-sitter grammar for CompMD, so editors can highlight and fold it.

## First, a design shown to the user

- How it sits on a Markdown grammar (CompMD is CommonMark + GFM): its own grammar, or injections on an existing tree-sitter Markdown grammar.
- What it covers: frontmatter and the `md` key, blocks (`:::`), inline components, interpolation (`{{…}}`) with CEL inside, the fences of component definitions with their languages injected, and the opt-in syntax.
- Where it lives and how it's published (npm and crates.io, as tree-sitter grammars are), and which editors to try it in.

## Then

Build it, with tests from the spec's examples and test suite, so it parses what the spec says.

## Notes

Each push needs the user's go.

## From earlier work

- A first design (`docs/tree-sitter.md`, compmd `b8809c7`: two grammars extending tree-sitter-markdown's by inheritance, its C scanner copied with CompMD's lines, CEL injected from a small tree-sitter-cel, queries for highlight, fold, inject and textobjects, tests from the spec and the conformance set, in `tree-sitter/`, published to npm and crates.io) was replaced by the combined editor-support design, `docs/editor-support.md`. Build what that design says.
- Editors: VS Code, Neovim, Helix, Zed and Emacs, as the editor-support design decides.
- From CMD-37: a ` ```compmd ` block with `render=output` or `both` is an example (spec §7.8), a CompMD document of its own: inject CompMD into its text, as into a definition fence's. Its param list is a rendered block's (`render`, the common params, `class`, `id`).

tasks.name: A browser preview for editors
tasks.description:
Asked by the user (2026-11-17): the playground without its editor side, a page in the browser that shows one document as it renders, opened from each editor.

## What it is

- The playground's preview alone: the renderer and the sandbox on the document the writer has open, with its folder's files and packs, updated as they type.
- Served on `localhost` by the language server (CMD-24), which has the document's text as it changes; the server offers it as a command and a code action (*Open preview*), so it works in every editor with a language server client, Helix too, and an editor package adds a button or a key where its editor has one.
- Follows the writer: the preview scrolls to the part being edited.

## First

graph LR; draft --> review --> published
